content: When cleaning areas contaminated by rodents, it is essential to wear protective gloves made of rubber, latex, vinyl, or nitrile. Rodent urine and droppings should be sprayed with a disinfectant or a chlorine solution until they are thoroughly soaked. This step is critical to prevent the generation of potentially infectious aerosols. Avoid vacuuming or sweeping rodent-contaminated surfaces until they have been disinfected. Use a paper towel to pick up the urine and droppings, and dispose of the paper towel in the garbage. After removing the droppings and urine, disinfect any items or surfaces that may have been contaminated by rodents. Floors should be mopped with a disinfectant or a chlorine solution. A homemade chlorine solution can be prepared by mixing 1½ cups of household bleach with 1 gallon of water (a 1:10 solution). When using chlorine solutions, take care to avoid spilling the mixture on clothing or other items that could be damaged by bleach. Always wear protective gloves when preparing and using chlorine solutions, and ensure that the solutions are prepared fresh daily. When cleaning closed sheds or other outbuildings, ventilate the area by opening doors and windows for at least 30 minutes before beginning the cleaning process. Cross-ventilation is recommended if possible. Leave the area during the airing-out period to allow the removal of infectious primary aerosols that may be present, particularly if hantavirus-infected rodents have urinated in the space. In environments that are heavily soiled or dusty, additional protective clothing or equipment, such as disposable coveralls and safety glasses or goggles, should be worn in addition to gloves. For buildings with heavy rodent infestations, special precautions are necessary. Heavy infestations are characterized by large accumulations of feces, numerous nests, or the presence of dead rodents. Individuals tasked with cleaning such areas should contact local or state public health agencies or the CDC for specific guidance. These precautions also apply to vacant dwellings that have attracted rodents while unoccupied, as well as to structures previously occupied by individuals with confirmed hantavirus infection. Workers involved in cleanup efforts should receive thorough training on hantavirus transmission, disease symptoms, and safe cleaning practices from the responsible health agency or employer. The recommendations for cleaning homes or buildings with heavy rodent infestations are designed to minimize the risk of human exposure to hantavirus-infected rodents. These guidelines are applicable across different geographic areas, regardless of variations in housing types or rodent populations. The CDC and local health agencies will continue to review and update these recommendations as new epidemiologic, field, and laboratory data become available. Future modifications or supplements to these guidelines may be implemented as necessary.
